title: GOD WARNED THE KING ABOUT HIS WIVES—THEN SOLOMON DID THE VERY THING GOD SAID WOULD DESTROY HIM
paragraphs:
GOD WARNED THE KING ABOUT HIS WIVES—THEN SOLOMON DID THE VERY THING GOD SAID WOULD DESTROY HIM
Deuteronomy’s forgotten warning about power, women, wealth, and the human heart is not merely an ancient command for kings. It exposes something frightening about us all: you can possess wisdom, influence, success, and even a history with God—and still slowly give your heart to something that takes you away from Him.
There is a sentence buried in Deuteronomy that becomes almost unbearable when you know what happens later.
God was preparing Israel for a future they had not yet reached.
There was no magnificent royal palace in Jerusalem.
No golden throne.
No famous son of David surrounded by international dignitaries.
No temple glittering beneath the sun.
No Solomon.
Not yet.
But God already knew what power could do to a human heart.
And so, long before Israel's kings began collecting horses, treasures, political alliances, and wives, the Lord gave them a warning.
In Deuteronomy 17:17, speaking specifically about Israel's future king, the Hebrew says:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
V'lo yarbeh-lo nashim, v'lo yasur levavo.
In context, the sense is:
He must not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn aside.
Read those final words again.
Lest his heart turn aside.
That is the center of the warning.
God was not merely regulating the size of a royal household.
He was guarding the heart of the king.
And centuries later, one of the wisest men who ever lived would become a living tragedy of that very sentence.
Solomon.
The man who had wisdom.
The man who built the temple.
The man who experienced extraordinary blessing.
The man whose fame crossed borders.
The man kings and queens wanted to hear.
The man who seemingly had everything.
And yet there came a point when everything was not enough.
That should frighten us more than it does.
Because some people imagine spiritual collapse begins when someone suddenly wakes up and decides, “Today I am going to abandon God.”
Usually it does not.
It begins smaller.
Another compromise.
Another appetite excused.
Another boundary moved.
Another affection allowed to become too powerful.
Another warning rationalized because nothing terrible happened yesterday.
Then another.
Then another.
Until something you once controlled begins controlling you.
Deuteronomy's warning about wives sits beside two other warnings for Israel's king.
He was not to multiply horses.
He was not to multiply wives.
He was not to excessively accumulate silver and gold.
Power.
Pleasure.
Possessions.
God knew the temptations surrounding the throne before Israel ever had a throne.
The king could begin thinking his security came from military strength.
His satisfaction from multiplying relationships.
His significance from accumulating wealth.
And underneath all three temptations was essentially the same lie:
God is not enough.
That lie is ancient.
And it is still destroying people.
You may never sit on a throne.
You may never command an army.
You may never possess Solomon's treasury.
You may never have hundreds of wives.
But you can still multiply the thing God warned you about.
Another drink.
Another purchase.
Another flirtation.
Another private conversation.
Another secret account.
Another fantasy.
Another achievement.
Another relationship you know is pulling your heart somewhere Jesus never asked it to go.
Another little kingdom where you are king and God is expected to remain silent.
And slowly...
וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
The heart turns aside.
That Hebrew word לְבָבוֹ — levavo refers to his heart, his inner person—the center of desire, allegiance, thought, and will.
That matters because the biblical problem is deeper than counting wives.
God was concerned about allegiance.
Who owns the heart?
Who sits at its center?
Who receives its deepest loyalty?
This also keeps us from twisting the passage into something it never says.
Deuteronomy 17:17 is not a license to despise women.
Women are not presented as some inherently corrupting class of people.
The command confronts the king.
He must not multiply wives.
His heart must not turn aside.
The responsibility rests on the ruler who refuses God's boundary.
And Scripture gives us another crucial piece of context when Solomon's story arrives.

First Kings 11 tells us that Solomon loved many foreign women and entered relationships with women from nations concerning whom Israel had been warned because of the danger of being drawn into the worship of their gods.
The central issue was not ethnicity as though God despised foreigners.
The Old Testament itself destroys that interpretation.
Ruth was a Moabite woman, yet through faithfulness to Israel's God she became part of the covenant community and even entered the genealogy leading to David—and ultimately to Jesus Christ.
Rahab was not born an Israelite either.
The biblical concern was covenant faithfulness and idolatry.
The danger was being drawn away from the living God.
And then Solomon's story becomes heartbreaking.
First Kings 11 records that Solomon eventually had seven hundred wives who were princesses and three hundred concubines.
One thousand women.
But the most terrifying number in the chapter is not one thousand.
The most terrifying thing is what happened to one heart.
His wives turned his heart away.
Exactly what God had warned about.
Long before Solomon's palace existed, God had effectively said:
Do not multiply wives...
lest your heart turn aside.
Then Solomon multiplied wives...
and his heart turned aside.
The warning became biography.
The command became tragedy.
And perhaps the most unsettling thing about Solomon's collapse is that wisdom did not make him immune.
You can know truth and still disobey truth.
You can explain Scripture and still resist Scripture.
You can recognize temptation in somebody else's life while quietly negotiating with it in your own.
You can have yesterday's testimony and today's compromise living under the same roof.
Knowing what God said is not the same as surrendering to what God said.
Solomon knew much.
But somewhere along the road, knowledge stopped governing desire.
And somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You know the verse.
You know the warning.
You know what the Holy Spirit has been pressing on your conscience.
You know that relationship is compromising you.
You know that secret habit is getting stronger.
You know that bitterness has lived inside you too long.
You know that what began as entertainment has become bondage.
You know that you keep telling yourself you can stop whenever you want.
You know.
And that is what makes this uncomfortable.
Sometimes our greatest spiritual danger is not ignorance.
Sometimes it is becoming comfortable disobeying something we already understand.
There are people who have not verbally rejected Jesus.
They simply keep adding competitors to Him.
Jesus...
plus my secret sin.
Jesus...
plus the approval I cannot live without.
Jesus...
plus the relationship I refuse to surrender.
Jesus...
plus money.
Jesus...
plus pornography.
Jesus...
plus status.
Jesus...
plus revenge.
Jesus...
plus the private version of me nobody at church knows exists.
Eventually the heart becomes divided.
And divided hearts do not usually announce their departure.
They drift.
Quietly.
Gradually.
Respectably.
Until one day the person looks back and realizes they have traveled miles from the place where they first compromised.
But Deuteronomy does not only tell the king what not to do.
It tells him what must keep him near God.

The king was instructed to possess a copy of God's law, keep it with him, and read it throughout his life so that he would learn to fear the LORD, carefully obey God's words, and prevent his heart from being lifted above his fellow Israelites.
Do you see the contrast?
The king could surround himself with possessions...
or surround his heart with God's Word.
He could multiply whatever fed his appetite...
or repeatedly return himself to the voice of God.
He could exalt himself...
or live underneath the authority of the LORD.
God's answer to royal arrogance was not more applause.
It was Scripture.
Read it.
Keep it near.
Remember who you are.
Remember who God is.
Remember that although people may call you king, you are still under the King.
And now the story reaches us.
Because the Bible's kings leave us longing for another King.
A King who would not be corrupted by power.
A King who could be offered the kingdoms of the world and refuse Satan's shortcut.
A King who would possess ultimate authority yet humble Himself.
A King who would not exploit people for pleasure but give Himself to rescue sinners.
A King who would not accumulate earthly treasure for Himself but become poor for our sake.
A King whose heart never turned away from His Father.
Jesus Christ.
Solomon possessed extraordinary wisdom and still failed.
Jesus is greater than Solomon.
Solomon built a temple.
Jesus spoke of the temple of His body and rose again.
Solomon sat on an earthly throne.
Jesus reigns as Lord.
Solomon's divided heart contributed to disaster in the kingdom.
Jesus came to rescue people with divided hearts and make rebels children of God.
This is where the story becomes more than a warning.
It becomes Gospel.
Because perhaps your heart has already wandered.
Perhaps this article did not catch you before the compromise.
Perhaps it found you afterward.
After the affair.
After the addiction.
After the lie.
After the divorce.
After the secret.
After the night you wish you could erase.
After the years you cannot recover.
After you ignored God's warning and discovered that sin always charges more than its advertisement promised.
Then hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more terribly than we like to admit.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is offered not because we can rewrite our past, but because Christ can redeem sinners who cannot repair themselves.
Repentance does not mean pretending the scandal never happened.
It means turning from sin toward the Savior.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace enters the darkness and brings the guilty person to Jesus.
Maybe you multiplied the wrong things.
Maybe your heart turned aside.
Maybe everyone sees the Christian version of you while God sees the exhausted person underneath it.
You do not need another performance.
You need Christ.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the greed.
Bring Him the relationship.
Bring Him the secret messages.
Bring Him the hidden browser history.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the part of your life you desperately hope nobody discovers.
Repent.
Not because Jesus is waiting to humiliate you.
Because sin is already destroying what Christ came to redeem.
There is mercy for the repentant sinner.
There is forgiveness through Christ.
There is no scandal so powerful that it can somehow make the blood of Jesus insufficient for the person who truly comes to Him.
That does not make sin small.
It makes Christ glorious.
So ask yourself the question Deuteronomy quietly forces upon every generation:
What am I multiplying that is slowly turning my heart away from God?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit with it.
Maybe it is not obviously sinful.
Maybe it is something good that became ultimate.
Career.
Money.
Romance.
Recognition.
Ministry.
Followers.
Comfort.
Success.
Even good things become dangerous when they demand the place belonging to God.
Maybe the Holy Spirit has already put something in your mind.
Be honest.
Not as a magic phrase.
Not as a public performance.
Let it be the beginning of honesty.
Someone else reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only person struggling to remain faithful.
Sometimes three words are enough to stop pretending.
And if Christ has already been restoring areas of your life you thought were permanently ruined, tell somebody.
Your testimony might become another person's reason not to surrender to despair tonight.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. We are saved by God's grace through faith in Christ.
They know the warnings.
They love God with part of themselves.
But something else is slowly taking the throne.
They may never tell you.
There may come a night when the temptation you thought you defeated comes knocking again, and you need to remember:
Do not keep multiplying what is turning your heart away from God.
Not because God can be bought.
Not because financial support earns salvation or blessing.
But because when believers freely support Gospel-centered work they genuinely value, they help that work keep reaching people.

If you want to glorify God through your support, do it with the right heart: not purchasing favor from Him, but freely helping biblical content reach another exhausted believer, another wandering heart, another curious unbeliever, another person hiding behind a smile.
Not to prove your faith.
Not to manipulate God into blessing you.
Share because truth travels when somebody is willing to carry it.
There could be someone in your circle standing one compromise away from a disaster they cannot yet see.
Let the warning reach them before the consequences do.
Because that is ultimately what Deuteronomy's warning about kings and wives reveals.
God saw the danger before Solomon did.
God gave the warning before Solomon broke it.
And God was right.
The horses could not save him.
The gold could not satisfy him.
The women could not complete him.
The wisdom could not excuse him.
The throne could not protect his heart.
And none of the things you are tempted to put in God's place can save you either.
There is only one King who can carry the full weight of your worship.
Jesus.
So whatever has been multiplying...
whatever has been quietly competing...
whatever has been pulling...
whatever has been sitting on the throne of your heart pretending it belongs there...
bring it down.
Return to Christ.
Because the most dangerous thing Solomon multiplied was not ultimately horses, gold, or wives.
It was distance between his heart and God.
And perhaps the greatest mercy God can give you today is allowing you to recognize that distance before it becomes your story.
Come home while you can still hear His voice calling.
Come home with the scandal.
Come home with the shame.
Come home with the consequences.
Come home without excuses.
Come to Jesus.
Because your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
The heart that wandered does not need a better hiding place—it needs to come home to its King.
